title: Overview and justification
body:
By now you should be comfortable with the basics of referencing: naming sources, matching a style, and spotting an inconsistent citation. This course builds on that. It moves from getting referencing right to judging it: checking a paraphrase properly against its original, weighing whether a reference list's range reflects the real scope of someone's research, and working out how to reference a source that does not fit a standard template.

By the end you will be able to check a paraphrase against its source, judge whether a reference list's range reflects real research scope, and paraphrase a technical passage for a non-specialist reader. You will also work out what an unfamiliar source needs, reference it correctly under time pressure, and gather and cite sources that both support and challenge a position.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this course, you will be able to:

  • Analyse a paraphrase against its original source to check that no distinctive wording survives unattributed.
  • Evaluate a reference list to judge whether its range, including opposing views, reflects the genuine scope of the research undertaken.
  • Paraphrase a technical passage accurately for a non-specialist reader, marking any direct quotation and crediting the source throughout.
  • Analyse an unfamiliar source type to identify which elements a reader needs to locate it, rather than forcing it into a standard template.
  • Reference an unfamiliar source type correctly under time pressure, checking guidance and recording the decision so the approach can be repeated.
  • Gather and cite sources that both support and challenge a position, so a reader can judge the breadth of research behind a recommendation.

title: In real academic practice
body: Checking a paraphrase, judging a reference list's range, and working out how to cite something unfamiliar are not one-off exam skills: you will meet them across every module that asks for independent reading, from literature reviews to group projects with mixed source types. The judgement you build here also feeds directly into how you handle sources when researching and when writing critically, where the same questions about range, attribution and traceability come up again.

title: Signpost
body: The course has six short lessons. First, checking a paraphrase against its original source. Second, judging whether a reference list's range reflects real research scope. Third, paraphrasing a technical passage for a non-specialist reader. Fourth, working out what an unfamiliar source type needs. Fifth, referencing an unfamiliar source correctly under time pressure. Sixth, gathering and citing sources that support and challenge a position. Work through them in order; each builds on the one before.
instruction: Work through the six lessons in order.

title: Course instructions
body:
Start and finish with a confidence check. Before the lessons, you'll rate how confident you feel about each part of this topic. You'll rate the same statements again at the end, so you can see what has changed. Your ratings are yours: they aren't marked and no one else sees them.

The activities in the lessons are for practice. Questions, examples and reflective prompts are there to help you think, and they don't count towards passing. Reflective prompts are private and optional.

The test at the end is the one that counts. To complete the course you need to take the final test and score at least 70%. You can retake it.

title: How this course works
body:
The examples and activities in this course use invented people, authors and sources to show how things work. Unless we say otherwise, any name, citation or reference you meet in an example is fictional.

Where a lesson draws on real work, you'll find it listed under Lesson Sources at the bottom of that page. Every real source used in the course is gathered under Course Sources at the end.

title: Orientation
body: This course moves from the mechanics of a reference to the judgement calls referencing demands. This lesson starts with paraphrase: writing an idea in your own words well enough that nothing of the original survives unattributed.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this stage, the aim is to compare a paraphrase against its source closely enough to catch wording that has survived, and to revise it so nothing has.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • compare a paraphrase against its original source
  • identify distinctive wording surviving unattributed in a paraphrase
  • revise a paraphrase so no wording survives unattributed

title: Concept: definition
body: A paraphrase restates an idea in the writer's own words and sentence structure, citing the source. Checking a paraphrase means comparing it sentence by sentence against the original, looking for any distinctive phrase, order or structure that has survived unattributed, even when the source is cited correctly. A citation credits the idea; it does not excuse wording that is still, in effect, the original author's.

title: Moving into practice
body: You have seen what a paraphrase needs to leave behind and what counts as wording surviving unattributed. The activities ahead let you practise spotting it and fixing it; the check at the end asks you to apply both.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Find a paraphrase you have written recently and put it side by side with its original source. Does any distinctive phrase or sentence structure survive?

No right answers apply here; the aim is simply to see how closely your own paraphrasing tracks the original.

title: Summary
body: You can now compare a paraphrase against its source, identify wording that has survived unattributed, and revise a paraphrase so nothing has. The next lesson turns to judging the range of a reference list as a whole.

_items.title: See pages 193 to 195 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: You have already checked that a reference list uses a consistent style and that each citation points to the right entry. This lesson asks a different question: does the list, taken as a whole, actually reflect the research it claims to draw on? A reference list can be perfectly formatted and still be thin, one-sided, or out of date, and none of that shows up in a style check.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level you are not just reading a reference list; you are judging it. Given a reference list and the claim it is supposed to support, you will decide whether the list's range is wide enough, whether it includes views that disagree with the writer's own, and where the evidence coverage falls short.

title: Learning outcomes
body: A reference list earns a reader's trust by its range, not just its formatting. When you judge whether a reference list includes opposing views, whether its range matches its claimed scope, and where it leaves evidence gaps, you are reading the way an examiner or reviewer reads. You are checking for what the writer chose not to cite, as much as for what they did.

title: Moving into practice
body: Judging a reference list this way becomes second nature once you have done it a few times. Before you accept a reference list at face value, in your own reading or someone else's, ask what range it covers, whether disagreement is represented, and what it leaves out.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a reading list or reference list you have used recently, for an assignment or a piece of research. Does it include views that disagree with the argument it supports? Is there a gap in evidence coverage you noticed at the time, or only now? No right answers are expected here; the aim is to look at the list itself, not just the argument it was attached to.

title: Summary
body: A reference list's range matters as much as its formatting. Check whether it includes opposing views, whether its range matches the scope it claims, and where it leaves evidence gaps. A well-formatted list that fails all three still misrepresents the research behind it.

_items.title: See pages 191 to 193 of Chapter 10, 'Academic Integrity and Referencing', of Excelling at University by Dennis and Abbott (2026).

title: Orientation
body: So far you have paraphrased material written at roughly the level you are writing at. This lesson asks you to paraphrase a technical passage for a reader who does not share the writer's specialist vocabulary, while still crediting the source accurately throughout and marking anywhere you keep a phrase word for word.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level the challenge is not just avoiding the original wording; it is making a technical passage make sense to someone new to the field, without losing the source's meaning or its credit. You will decide what needs explaining, what can be kept as a direct quotation, and how to credit the source at more than one point in a longer paraphrase.

title: Learning outcomes
body: Paraphrasing for a new reader means rewriting a technical passage in plain terms while keeping its meaning intact and its source credited. Where a technical term has no everyday equivalent, or the original phrasing is too precise to improve on, you quote it directly rather than force an imprecise paraphrase. Across a longer passage, you credit the source more than once, not only at the first sentence, so a reader never loses track of whose idea they are reading.

title: Moving into practice
body: Paraphrasing for a non-specialist becomes more natural with practice. Before you paraphrase a technical passage, identify the terms a new reader will not know, decide which phrases are precise enough to quote directly, and plan where you will credit the source again as the passage continues.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a technical passage from your own subject that you have paraphrased, or will need to, for a reader outside the field. Which terms would need explaining? Is there a phrase precise enough that quoting it directly would serve the reader better than paraphrasing it? No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice where plain language and precision pull against each other.

title: Summary
body: Paraphrasing a technical passage for a new reader means rewriting it in plain terms, marking any phrase kept as a direct quotation, and crediting the source more than once across a longer passage. Losing any one of these loses either the reader or the source.

title: Orientation
body: Every referencing style covers the common source types: books, journal articles, websites. Sooner or later you will meet a source that does not fit any of these cleanly: a dataset, a piece of software, a recorded lecture, a government report with no named author. This lesson is about working out what that source needs, rather than forcing it into the nearest template.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level the task is analysis, not lookup. Given an unfamiliar source, you will identify what a reader needs in order to find it again: who or what produced it, when, where it can be accessed, and what distinguishes this instance from any other. You will also recognise when forcing it into a standard template loses information a reader needs.

title: Learning outcomes
body: An unfamiliar source type is one your referencing style's examples do not cover directly: a dataset, a piece of software, a recording, a report with a corporate rather than a named author. Working out how to cite it means identifying the elements any citation needs, whatever the source, and finding where this source carries each one, even if its label is unfamiliar.

title: Moving into practice
body: Meeting an unfamiliar source stops being daunting once you know what to look for. Before you cite a source your style guide does not cover directly, identify who or what produced it, when, where it can be accessed, and what would let a reader find this exact instance again.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a source you have used, or expect to use, that does not fit neatly into "book", "journal article", or "website": a dataset, a recording, a report, a piece of software. What elements would a reader need to find it again? Is there a version or date that distinguishes this instance from others? No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice what the source itself offers, not what a template expects it to offer.

title: Summary
body: Citing an unfamiliar source means identifying what any citation needs, whatever the source type, and finding where this source carries each element, even under an unfamiliar label. Forcing it into a standard template instead risks losing exactly the information a reader needs to find it again.

title: Orientation
body: You can now work out how to cite an unfamiliar source when you have time to think it through. This lesson is about doing the same thing under pressure: a deadline, a source you only just found, no time to check every detail. Referencing correctly under pressure is not about skipping steps; it is about knowing which steps you can do quickly and recording what you decided.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level the challenge is speed without sacrificing accuracy. Given an unfamiliar source and limited time, you will reference it correctly, check the guidance that applies when you are unsure, and record the decision you made so you, or someone else, can repeat it or correct it later.

title: Learning outcomes
body: Referencing under pressure means applying the same four elements (producer, date, access, distinguishing detail) quickly rather than skipping them. When a style guide does not give a direct example, checking its general guidance, rather than guessing, still takes less time than researching from scratch. Recording the decision, in a note or a source log, means you are not working it out again if the same source appears later.

title: Moving into practice
body: Referencing under pressure gets faster with a routine. When time is short, apply the four elements quickly, check general guidance rather than guessing if you are unsure, and write down the decision you made before you move on.

title: Reflective prompt
body: Think of a time you had to reference a source quickly, close to a deadline. Did you check guidance when unsure, or guess? Did you record the decision anywhere, or would you have to work it out again if the source came up a second time? No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice what you actually did under pressure, not what you would do with more time.

title: Summary
body: Referencing under pressure still means applying the four elements, checking guidance rather than guessing when unsure, and recording the decision so it can be repeated or corrected. Speed does not excuse skipping any of the three.

title: Orientation
body: A literature review or a position paper is judged partly on its breadth. A reference list that cites only sources agreeing with the writer's position looks selective, even when every citation is accurate. Readers, markers and peer reviewers expect to see sources that challenge a position as well as sources that support it, because that balance is what shows the writer has engaged with the real state of the evidence rather than picked out what suited them.

title: Orientation: at this level
body: At this level, you are not just finding sources: you are building a reference list that demonstrates you have surveyed a debate, not just picked a side. Gathering sources that challenge your position before you finalise an argument lets you address counter-evidence directly instead of having a reader raise it for you.

title: Learning outcomes
body:
By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:

  • Gather sources that support a position.
  • Gather sources that challenge a position.
  • Cite opposing sources so a reader can judge research breadth.

title: Concept: definition
body: Citing both sides means deliberately including sources that argue against your position alongside those that support it, each cited accurately enough that a reader can trace and judge the breadth of research behind your argument. It is not about abandoning a position; it is about showing you reached it after weighing opposing evidence, not instead of it.

title: Moving into practice
body: You now know how to build a reference list that shows research breadth rather than selective citation. The next step is applying this across a whole piece of work: as you draft, keep a running note of which sources support your argument and which challenge it, and check periodically that both lists are growing, not just one.

title: Reflective prompt
body:
Think of a time you argued for a position in an assignment. Did you actively search for sources that disagreed with you, or did you mainly collect sources that confirmed what you already thought? What would change in your search process if you deliberately gathered opposing evidence first?

No right answers are expected here; the aim is to notice your own habit before you write your next argument.

title: Summary
body: A reference list that cites only supporting sources looks selective, however accurate each citation is. Gathering sources that challenge your position, not only sources that support it, is what lets a reader judge the real breadth of your research. Citing an opposing source accurately, with enough detail to trace it, shows you engaged with the counter-evidence rather than ignored it.

title: Assessment introduction
body:
This is the test for the whole course. It covers everything you've studied in the lessons, with a set of questions to work through.

To pass, you need to score at least 70%. You can retake the test if you don't pass first time.

title: Course summary
body: You have reached the end of the course. Referencing is no longer just about getting the mechanics right. You can now check a paraphrase against its source, judge whether a reference list's range reflects the real scope of someone's research, and paraphrase a technical passage for a non-specialist reader. You can also work out what an unfamiliar source needs, reference it correctly under time pressure, and gather sources that support and challenge a position. That judgement builds directly on the accuracy and consistency you brought from the introductory course. Look back at the confidence check to see how far this has moved.

title: In real academic practice
body: Apply this judgement the next time you draft a literature review or a group report with mixed source types. Check your own paraphrases against their originals, weigh whether your reading list's range reflects the scope of the question, and work out an unfamiliar source's citation from first principles rather than forcing it into a template. The same judgement about range and traceability is exactly what you draw on when finding and using sources for a longer project, and when researching a topic that calls for a documented method.

title: Where this goes next
body: This course has assumed the introductory groundwork: naming sources accurately, matching a style, and spotting an inconsistent citation. If any of that still feels shaky, the introductory course is there to revisit. Moving on, the advanced course in this pathway turns from getting the judgement right to acting on it under pressure: the ethical choices that referencing and attribution raise once you are working independently, in shared work, or in a professional role.

body: A student rewrites a source sentence by swapping a few words but keeping its structure and most phrasing. What should checking the paraphrase against its original reveal?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does checking a paraphrase against its original reveal here?

_items.text: That distinctive wording from the original survives unattributed, so it isn't yet a genuine paraphrase.
_items.feedback: Yes. Checking against the original shows whether its distinctive wording still survives unattributed.

_items.text: That the sentence is now too short to need a citation at all.
_items.feedback: Length doesn't remove the need to credit the source; wording and attribution do.

_items.text: That changing any words at all makes it sufficiently different from the source.
_items.feedback: A few swapped words can still leave the original's structure and phrasing intact.

_items.text: That the citation can simply move to the end of the paragraph instead.
_items.feedback: Where the citation sits doesn't address whether the wording is genuinely paraphrased.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Checking against the original shows whether its distinctive wording still survives unattributed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Compare the structure and phrasing, not just whether any words changed.

body: A reference list cites several sources that all support the same conclusion, with no opposing view represented. What does evaluating its range suggest?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does evaluating this reference list's range suggest?

_items.text: The range may not reflect the genuine scope of research into the topic.
_items.feedback: Yes. A one-sided list may understate how much research actually exists on the topic.

_items.text: The list is too short to meet a minimum reference count.
_items.feedback: Count alone doesn't show whether the research's real scope is reflected.

_items.text: The sources are too old to be considered current research.
_items.feedback: Age isn't stated here; the issue described is one-sidedness, not currency.

_items.text: The citation style used is inconsistent across the entries.
_items.feedback: Style consistency is a separate issue from whether the range reflects the topic's scope.

_feedback.correct: That's right. A list with no opposing view may not reflect the genuine scope of research into the topic.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what's missing from the list, not its length or style.

body: You are paraphrasing a technical passage for a reader unfamiliar with the field. What must the paraphrase still do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What must a technical paraphrase for a new reader still do?

_items.text: Credit the source throughout and mark any direct quotation, even in plain language.
_items.feedback: Yes. Simplifying the language doesn't remove the need to credit the source and mark any quotation.

_items.text: Avoid citing the source since the wording is now entirely your own.
_items.feedback: The ideas still come from the source, so it still needs crediting.

_items.text: Keep the original technical terms exactly as written, regardless of the reader.
_items.feedback: The task is to make the passage accessible, not to preserve every technical term.

_items.text: Cite the source once at the very end of the whole passage.
_items.feedback: A single end citation doesn't mark which parts are direct quotation throughout.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Even in plain language, the paraphrase must credit the source and mark any direct quotation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Simplifying the wording doesn't change what attribution the passage still needs.

body: You need to reference an unfamiliar source type with no obvious template. What should you identify first?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you identify first for an unfamiliar source type?

_items.text: Which elements a reader would need to locate the source themselves.
_items.feedback: Yes. Starting from what a reader needs to locate the source works for any source type.

_items.text: Which existing template looks closest, even if it doesn't quite fit.
_items.feedback: Forcing an ill-fitting template risks leaving out what this source actually needs.

_items.text: Whether the source type is common enough to be worth citing.
_items.feedback: Commonness doesn't determine how to construct the reference itself.

_items.text: How many other students have cited the same source type before.
_items.feedback: Precedent from other students doesn't tell you what this reference needs.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Identifying what a reader needs to locate the source works from first principles, for any source type.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what the reference is actually for, not which template is nearest.

body: You must reference an unfamiliar source type under time pressure. What should you do, beyond getting an answer quickly?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should you do when referencing under time pressure?

_items.text: Check the guidance and record the decision so the approach can be repeated.
_items.feedback: Yes. Recording the decision means you don't have to work it out again next time.

_items.text: Use whichever format looks reasonable and move on without recording it.
_items.feedback: An unrecorded guess leaves you with nothing to check or repeat later.

_items.text: Skip the citation for now and add it only if someone asks.
_items.feedback: Skipping it risks the citation never being added at all.

_items.text: Copy the format used for a different, more familiar source type.
_items.feedback: Borrowing a format from an unrelated source type risks missing what this one needs.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Checking guidance and recording the decision means the approach can be repeated next time.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what you'd need the next time you meet the same source type.

body: A recommendation is backed only by sources that agree with it. What does gathering and citing opposing sources as well let a reader do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does citing opposing sources as well let a reader do?

_items.text: Judge the breadth of research behind the recommendation.
_items.feedback: Yes. Seeing both sides lets a reader judge how broad the research behind it really is.

_items.text: See that the recommendation has no real weaknesses at all.
_items.feedback: Citing opposing views doesn't remove weaknesses; it lets a reader weigh them.

_items.text: Assume the writer simply ran out of supporting evidence to cite.
_items.feedback: Including opposing sources is a deliberate choice, not a sign of running short.

_items.text: Skip reading the opposing sources, since they are only there for balance.
_items.feedback: They are there to be read and weighed, not skipped as decoration.

_feedback.correct: That's right. Citing sources on both sides lets a reader judge the real breadth of research behind the recommendation.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Think about what a reader gains from seeing opposing evidence included.

title: Activity: faithful paraphrase or surviving wording
body: Three paraphrases, each checked against its original sentence.
instruction: Select an option for each item, then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Classify each paraphrase as faithful or as having distinctive wording survive unattributed.

_items.text: Original: 'Students who log sources immediately cite more accurately.' Paraphrase: 'Dennis and Abbott (2026) found that recording sources straight away leads to more accurate citing.'

Original: 'A reference should give a reader everything needed to find the exact source.' Paraphrase: 'A reference should give a reader everything needed to find the exact source, according to Dennis and Abbott (2026).'

Original: 'Mixed citation styles force a reader to re-learn the pattern with every entry.' Paraphrase: 'When styles are mixed, Dennis and Abbott (2026) note that a reader must work out a fresh pattern for every entry.'

_feedback.correct: That's right. A citation does not excuse a sentence structure or phrase lifted almost word for word from the original.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not quite. Compare the sentence structure, not just the individual words, against the original.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some of these are right, but not all. Check the rest.

title: Activity: steps for checking a paraphrase
body: These are the steps for checking a paraphrase against its source. They are out of order.
instruction: Drag items to reorder, or use the keyboard (Enter to grab, arrows to move, Enter to drop). Then select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Put the steps for checking a paraphrase against its source in the correct order.

_items.text: Place the paraphrase next to the original passage.
Read both, sentence by sentence.
Mark any phrase or structure that closely tracks the original.
Rewrite each marked section in genuinely different wording and structure.

_feedback.correct: That is the right order: compare side by side first, read closely, mark what survives, then rewrite it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Not in order yet. You need both passages side by side before you can compare them. Try again.

_partlyCorrect.notFinal: Some steps are in the right place, but not all. Try again.

title: Worked example: checking a paraphrase properly
displayTitle: Worked example: checking a paraphrase properly
body:
Two students each paraphrase the same sentence from a source and cite it.

{{learner-a}} swaps a few words for synonyms but keeps the original sentence structure almost exactly, then adds a citation at the end. The citation is correct, but the sentence is still, in effect, the original author's.

{{learner-b}} reads the original, closes the book, and writes the idea out in a different structure entirely, checking the result against the original afterward to confirm nothing distinctive has survived.

Only {{learner-b}}'s version is a genuine paraphrase; {{learner-a}}'s citation does not make a reworded original into one.

title: Activity: signs wording has survived
body: Four signs that distinctive wording has survived unattributed in a paraphrase. Select a card to flip it and see it explained.
instruction: Select each card to turn it over.

back.body: The order of clauses and ideas matches the original almost exactly, even if some words have changed.
A memorable or unusual turn of phrase from the original appears without quotation marks.
Individual words are replaced but the sentence otherwise reads the same as the original.
The same examples appear in the same order, suggesting the structure was copied rather than rethought.

title: Activity: revising a paraphrase properly
body: Four ways to revise a paraphrase so nothing survives unattributed. Open each to see it explained.
instruction: Select each heading to reveal it. Work through all four.

_items.title: Read, then write from memory
_items.body: Read the original, set it aside, and write the idea from memory rather than reworking the sentence in front of you.

_items.title: Change the structure, not just the words
_items.body: Reorder the clauses or combine separate sentences, rather than swapping words within the same structure.

_items.title: Quote anything you cannot improve on
_items.body: If a phrase genuinely cannot be bettered, put it in quotation marks instead of disguising it as a paraphrase.

_items.title: Check side by side before finishing
_items.body: Compare the finished paraphrase against the original once more, specifically looking for anything that still matches too closely.

title: Practical guidance: checking a paraphrase
body: Run through this list for every paraphrase in a piece of writing.
instruction: Tick each item once you have checked it.

_items.text: You have compared the paraphrase against the original, sentence by sentence.
No sentence structure closely tracks the original, even where words have changed.
Any phrase too distinctive to rewrite is quoted directly instead.
The source is cited, and the wording is genuinely your own.

title: Check 1: comparing a paraphrase
displayTitle: A paraphrase keeps the original's sentence structure, swapping only a few words, and cites the source. Is this an acceptable paraphrase?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: Is a paraphrase that keeps the original's structure but cites the source acceptable?

_items.text: No, because the sentence structure still belongs to the original author, regardless of the citation.
_items.feedback: Yes. A citation credits the idea; it does not excuse a structure that is still effectively the original author's.

_items.text: Yes, because the source is cited correctly.
_items.feedback: Citing the source is necessary but not sufficient; the wording and structure must also genuinely be the writer's own.

_items.text: Yes, because some words have been changed.
_items.feedback: Changing a few words while keeping the same structure does not make the sentence a genuine paraphrase.

_items.text: No, because citations are not needed for paraphrases.
_items.feedback: A paraphrase does need a citation; the problem here is the surviving structure, not the presence of a citation.

_feedback.correct: Yes. The structure still belongs to the original author; a citation alone does not make it an acceptable paraphrase.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what a citation does and does not excuse.
_incorrect.final: The structure still belongs to the original author; citing the source does not excuse that, and synonym-swapping does not create a genuine paraphrase.

title: Check 2: identifying surviving wording
displayTitle: A paraphrase uses a distinctive phrase from the original word for word, without quotation marks, but cites the source. What is this an example of?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What does using a distinctive unquoted phrase from the original show?

_items.text: Distinctive wording surviving unattributed, because the exact phrase is used without quotation marks.
_items.feedback: Yes. A distinctive phrase used word for word needs quotation marks, however the source is cited.

_items.text: A correctly formatted citation.
_items.feedback: The citation format is not the issue; the exact phrase needs quotation marks.

_items.text: A summary rather than a paraphrase.
_items.feedback: This is still presented as a paraphrase; the problem is the exact phrase surviving unquoted.

_items.text: An acceptable paraphrase, since the source is credited.
_items.feedback: Crediting the source does not excuse an exact phrase appearing without quotation marks.

_feedback.correct: Yes. An exact phrase without quotation marks is distinctive wording surviving unattributed, whatever the citation says.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what quotation marks are for, separately from the citation.
_incorrect.final: The exact phrase needs quotation marks; the citation format, calling it a summary, and crediting the source do not resolve this.

title: Check 3: revising a paraphrase
displayTitle: In a piece of work for {{context}}, your paraphrase still follows the original's sentence order after a first attempt. What should you do?
instruction: Choose one option and select Submit.
ariaQuestion: What should be done when a paraphrase still follows the original's sentence order?

_items.text: Set the original aside and rewrite the idea in a different structure from memory.
_items.feedback: Yes. Rewriting from memory, in a different structure, is how surviving wording gets removed.

_items.text: Add a second citation to the same sentence.
_items.feedback: A second citation does not change the sentence structure that is the actual problem.

_items.text: Shorten the sentence so less of it matches.
_items.feedback: Shortening the sentence does not address the structure still tracking the original.

_items.text: Leave it, since the idea is correctly credited.
_items.feedback: Credit alone does not resolve a structure that still tracks the original too closely.

_feedback.correct: Yes. Rewriting from memory in a different structure is the fix for wording that still tracks the original.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what actually changes the sentence structure, rather than the citation or the length.
_incorrect.final: Rewriting from memory, in a different structure, is the fix. A second citation, shortening, or leaving it do not address the structure itself.

title: Does this reference list include opposing views?
instruction: Match each reference list description to a judgement about its range.

_items.text: A list that cites five studies all reaching the same conclusion, on a question where the field is known to disagree
A list that cites the leading study and a direct rebuttal of it, alongside supporting work
A list that cites only sources published by the same research group as the writer

_feedback.correct: Right. A reference list that cites only agreement, or only one group's own work, has not represented the field's disagreement, whatever its formatting looks like.

_incorrect.notFinal: Look again at who is being cited, not just how many sources there are. Agreement in number is not the same as a represented range of views.

title: Judging a reference list's range
instruction: Put these steps for judging a reference list's range in order.

_items.text: Note what the writer claims the research covers
List the sources actually cited and what each one covers
Check whether disagreement in the field is represented
Identify what the claimed scope implies that is missing

_feedback.correct: Right. Scope first, then what is actually there, then whether disagreement features, then what the gap between the two implies.

_incorrect.notFinal: Start from what the writer claims to cover before checking what is actually cited; otherwise you are judging the list against nothing.

title: Reading a reference list for its range
body:
{{learner-a}} is asked to check a reference list attached to an essay claiming to cover "current debate on remote work productivity". {{learner-a}} counts the sources: eleven, all recent, all from business journals. {{learner-a}} decides the list is strong because there are enough sources and they all look current.

{{learner-b}} is asked to check the same list. {{learner-b}} starts from the claim, not the count: debate implies disagreement. Reading the eleven sources, {{learner-b}} finds they all report the same finding, that remote work increases productivity, and none test or challenge it. {{learner-b}} concludes the list is one-sided: it supports a claim of debate while containing none, whatever its size and recency.

title: Four signs a reference list's range falls short
instruction: Select each card to reveal a sign a reference list's range does not match its claimed scope.

_items.title: Only agreement
_items.body: Every source reaches the same conclusion, on a question the field is known to contest.

_items.title: Only one source type
_items.body: A claim about practice is supported only by theory, or a claim about theory only by anecdote.

_items.title: Only one group's own work
_items.body: The citations all trace back to the same research team or institution.

_items.title: Scope narrower than the claim
_items.body: The writer claims a broad review but the citations cover only a narrow slice of it.

title: Four ways to identify an evidence gap
instruction: Select each heading to reveal a way to identify an evidence gap in a reference list.

_items.title: Compare the claim to the citations
_items.body: State what the writer says the research covers, then list what the citations actually cover; the difference is the gap.

_items.title: Check for a missing source type
_items.body: A claim resting only on theory with no empirical support, or the reverse, has a gap in evidence type.

_items.title: Check the date range
_items.body: A claim about a fast-moving field supported only by older sources may have a currency gap.

_items.title: Check for the obvious rebuttal
_items.body: If a well-known challenge to the claim exists and is not cited, that absence is itself a gap.

title: Checking a reference list's range
body:
Use this checklist when judging a reference list:

  1. State what the writer claims the research covers.
  2. List what the cited sources actually cover.
  3. Check whether views that disagree with the writer's own are represented.
  4. Identify anything the claimed scope implies that is missing from the list.

title: Check your understanding
body: A reference list cites eleven recent sources, all reaching the same conclusion on a question the field is known to contest. What does this most strongly suggest?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: The list is strong, because eleven sources is a large number
The list's range does not match a contested question, because it represents no disagreement
The list is strong, because all sources are recent
The list cannot be judged without knowing the authors' institutions

_feedback.correct: Right. On a contested question, uniform agreement across every cited source is itself evidence that the list's range is too narrow, not a sign of strength.
_feedback._incorrect: Count and recency do not establish range. A list that cites only one side of a known disagreement has not matched the field's actual shape, however many sources it contains.

title: Check your understanding
body: An essay claims to give "a full review of theories of motivation" but every source cited is a single textbook chapter summarising one theory. What is missing?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: Nothing; a textbook chapter is a reliable source for any claim
The range does not match the claimed scope: one summary cannot support a claim of a full review
The essay needs a longer reference list, regardless of what it contains
The source is too old to be used for this claim

_feedback.correct: Right. A claim of a full review commits the writer to a range of theories and sources; one textbook summary cannot deliver on that claim, however reliable it is on its own terms.
_feedback._incorrect: The problem here is range against the claim made, not the reliability or age of the one source cited.

title: Check your understanding
body: You are judging a reference list for {{context}}. The list cites recent studies supporting the main argument, but no study that tests or challenges it. What gap does this show?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: An evidence gap: no opposing or testing view is represented
No gap, provided every cited source is itself reliable
A formatting gap, because the citations may not follow a consistent style
A currency gap, because the sources are described as recent

_feedback.correct: Right. Recency and individual reliability do not supply disagreement. A list that cites only supporting evidence leaves an evidence gap at the point where a challenge should appear.
_feedback._incorrect: Reliability and recency are not the issue here. Look at what kind of evidence is missing: anything that tests or opposes the main argument.

title: Plain language or jargon?
instruction: Match each rewritten sentence to whether it suits a non-specialist reader.

_items.text: "The intervention produced a statistically significant reduction in attrition." rewritten as "The programme produced a reduction in attrition that was unlikely to be due to chance."
"The intervention produced a statistically significant reduction in attrition." rewritten as "The programme significantly affected attrition in a statistically meaningful way."
"Participants were recruited via stratified random sampling." rewritten as "People were chosen at random, in proportions matching the wider population."

_feedback.correct: Right. Plain language replaces the technical term with what it means, rather than keeping the term and adding a technical gloss around it.

_incorrect.notFinal: Check whether the rewrite has actually removed the technical term, or just added more words around it.

title: Paraphrasing a technical passage
instruction: Put these steps for paraphrasing a technical passage in order.

_items.text: Identify the terms a non-specialist reader will not know
Decide which phrases are precise enough to quote directly
Rewrite the rest in plain language without losing the meaning
Credit the source again at a natural point further into the passage

_feedback.correct: Right. Know what needs explaining before you decide what to quote, then write the plain-language version, then make sure credit continues through the passage.

_incorrect.notFinal: Start by identifying the unfamiliar terms; deciding what to quote or credit before that is working in the wrong order.

title: Paraphrasing for a reader outside the field
body:
{{learner-a}} paraphrases a passage on soil permeability for a general-studies assignment. {{learner-a}} replaces "hydraulic conductivity" with "conductivity rate" and leaves the rest of the sentence structure and technical density unchanged, crediting the source once at the start of the paragraph.

{{learner-b}} paraphrases the same passage. {{learner-b}} rewrites "hydraulic conductivity" as "how easily water moves through the soil" and keeps the original's precise figure as a direct quotation, because no plain restatement would be as exact. {{learner-b}} credits the source again partway through the paragraph, where the original argument resumes after the quoted figure.

title: Four signs a term needs explaining
instruction: Select each card to reveal a sign a term needs explaining for a non-specialist reader.

_items.title: No everyday equivalent
_items.body: The term names something a general reader has no plain-language word for.

_items.title: Different everyday meaning
_items.body: The term means something else in ordinary use, risking confusion if left unexplained.

_items.title: Carries a precise value
_items.body: The term packs in a specific measurement or threshold a plain restatement would blur.

_items.title: Field-specific shorthand
_items.body: The term stands in for a longer explanation that specialists already share but a new reader does not.

title: Four ways to keep the source credited
instruction: Select each heading to reveal a way to keep a source credited across a longer paraphrase.

_items.title: Credit at the start
_items.body: Name the source before the paraphrase begins, so the reader knows whose argument follows.

_items.title: Credit again mid-passage
_items.body: If the paraphrase runs more than a sentence or two, repeat the source's name or a clear "they also" to keep credit attached.

_items.title: Credit around a quotation
_items.body: When you quote directly within a paraphrase, attribute the quotation specifically, not just the surrounding paraphrase.

_items.title: Credit at a change of idea
_items.body: If the passage moves to a new point from the same source, mark that the source is still speaking, not a new, uncredited claim.

title: Paraphrasing a technical passage
body:
Use this checklist when paraphrasing a technical passage for a new reader:

  1. List the terms a non-specialist reader will not know.
  2. Decide which phrases are precise enough to quote directly.
  3. Rewrite the rest in plain language without losing the original meaning.
  4. Credit the source again at a natural point further into the passage.

title: Check your understanding
body: A technical passage states a precise statistical threshold. You are not confident a plain restatement would capture it exactly. What should you do?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: Quote the figure directly, crediting the source, rather than risk blurring it in paraphrase
Paraphrase it anyway; a close approximation is good enough for a non-specialist reader
Omit the figure, since a non-specialist reader will not need it
Paraphrase it and add the original figure in brackets without attribution

_feedback.correct: Right. Where paraphrase risks losing precision, a direct, credited quotation serves the reader and the source better than an approximation.
_feedback._incorrect: Precision that paraphrase cannot safely preserve is exactly when a direct, credited quotation is the better choice, not omission or an uncredited figure.

title: Check your understanding
body: A paraphrase of a long technical passage names the source in its first sentence, then continues for three more sentences restating the source's argument with no further mention of who is being paraphrased. What is missing?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: Nothing; naming the source once at the start is sufficient for the whole passage
A repeated credit partway through, so a reader does not mistake the later sentences for the writer's own claims
A direct quotation, since paraphrase alone is never sufficient over several sentences
A reference-list entry, since in-text credit is not required for paraphrase

_feedback.correct: Right. Over several sentences, a single credit at the start fades; crediting the source again partway through keeps the reader clear about whose argument they are reading.
_feedback._incorrect: The issue here is in-text credit continuing through the passage, not whether a quotation or reference-list entry is also needed.

title: Check your understanding
body: You are paraphrasing a technical passage from {{context}} for a reader new to the subject. Which approach best suits this reader?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: Replace technical terms with plain language, keep only genuinely untranslatable precision as direct quotation, and credit the source throughout
Keep the original technical terms, since a reader new to the subject will need to learn them anyway
Quote the whole passage directly, to avoid any risk of misrepresenting it
Paraphrase freely and credit the source only once, at the very end

_feedback.correct: Right. Plain language serves the new reader; reserving direct quotation for what paraphrase cannot safely carry, and crediting the source throughout, keeps both the reader and the source served.
_feedback._incorrect: Keeping jargon, quoting everything, or crediting only once each fail one side of the same balance: a new reader's understanding and the source's credit.

title: What does a reader need to find this source?
instruction: Match each unfamiliar source to the element a reader most needs in order to find it again.

_items.text: A dataset held in an open repository, updated periodically
A government report issued by a department with no named author
options: The issuing body, standing in for an author

_items.text: A recorded lecture delivered live and not published elsewhere
options: The date and context of the recording

_feedback.correct: Right. Each unfamiliar source still needs an identifiable producer, a time, and a way back to the exact instance; what changes is which element carries that information.

_incorrect.notFinal: Ask what would let a reader find this exact source again, not what label the source carries.

title: Analysing an unfamiliar source
instruction: Put these steps for analysing an unfamiliar source type in order.

_items.text: Identify who or what produced the source
Identify when it was produced or last updated
Identify where and how a reader can access it
Identify what distinguishes this instance from any other

_feedback.correct: Right. Producer, date, access, and distinguishing detail: the same four questions apply whatever the source type, in that order.

_incorrect.notFinal: Start from who or what produced the source; access and distinguishing detail depend on knowing that first.

title: Citing a source outside the usual templates
body:
{{learner-a}} needs to cite a government department's open dataset. {{learner-a}} cannot find an author's name, so forces the citation into the "book" template, leaving the author field blank and losing the department's name and the dataset's version number altogether.

{{learner-b}} needs to cite the same dataset. {{learner-b}} starts from what a reader needs: the issuing department stands in for the author, the dataset's version and access date stand in for a publication date, and the repository's permanent link stands in for a publisher. The citation looks unlike any of the style guide's worked examples, but it carries everything a reader needs to find the exact version {{learner-b}} used.

title: Four elements any citation needs
instruction: Select each card to reveal an element any citation needs, whatever the source type.

_items.title: A producer
_items.body: A person, team, or body responsible for the source, even if no individual is named.

_items.title: A date
_items.body: When the source was produced, issued, or last updated.

_items.title: An access route
_items.body: Where and how a reader can reach the source themselves.

_items.title: A distinguishing detail
_items.body: A version, edition, or identifier that singles out this instance from any other like it.

title: Four ways forcing a template fails
instruction: Select each heading to reveal a way forcing an unfamiliar source into a standard template fails.

_items.title: Blank author field
_items.body: Leaving the author blank loses the issuing body that should have stood in for it.

_items.title: Wrong date entirely
_items.body: Using a publication date template for a periodically updated source loses which version was actually used.

_items.title: No access route
_items.body: A book template has no field for a repository link, so the reader is left unable to locate the source.

_items.title: Lost version
_items.body: Treating a dataset like a static publication drops the version number a reader needs to reproduce the same figures.

title: Citing an unfamiliar source
body:
Use this checklist when citing a source your style guide does not cover directly:

  1. Identify who or what produced the source.
  2. Identify when it was produced or last updated.
  3. Identify where and how a reader can access it.
  4. Identify what distinguishes this instance from any other.

title: Check your understanding
body: A dataset has no named individual author, only an issuing research centre. What should the citation do?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: Name the research centre as the author, since it is the body responsible for the source
Leave the author field blank, since no individual is named
Cite it as an anonymous source
Omit authorship and cite only the dataset's title

_feedback.correct: Right. Any citation needs a producer; when no individual is named, the issuing body stands in for the author, rather than being treated as absent.
_feedback._incorrect: A dataset still has a producer, even without a named individual. The issuing body fills that role rather than leaving it blank, anonymous, or omitted.

title: Check your understanding
body: You need to cite a piece of software used to analyse your data, with no clear "author" and no publication date in the usual sense. What should guide the citation?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: What elements a reader needs to identify and access this exact version of the software
The nearest standard template, with any unavailable field left blank
Omitting the citation, since software is not normally referenced
A citation for the software's user manual instead

_feedback.correct: Right. Starting from what a reader needs to find this exact version works for software just as it does for any other unfamiliar source; the developer and the version number carry what author and date would carry elsewhere.
_feedback._incorrect: Forcing a standard template, omitting the citation, or citing the manual instead all lose the point: identifying what a reader needs to find this version of the software itself.

title: Check your understanding
body: You are citing an unfamiliar source for {{context}}, and no named individual author is given. What matters most for a reader trying to find this source again?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: That the citation carries a producer, a date, an access route, and a distinguishing detail, however the source is labelled
That the citation matches the exact format of the style guide's book example
That the source is cited as anonymous, since no individual author is given
That the citation is kept as short as possible, since the source is unusual

_feedback.correct: Right. The four elements, not the label or the nearest template, are what let a reader locate the exact source, whatever kind of source it is.
_feedback._incorrect: Matching a book template, treating the source as anonymous, or shortening the citation all risk losing one of the four elements a reader actually needs.

title: Guessing or checking guidance?
instruction: Match each action, taken under time pressure, to whether it checks guidance or guesses.

_items.text: Searching the style guide's general rules for "source with no named author" when an unfamiliar source has none
Picking whichever template looks closest and filling in the gaps without checking
Applying the four elements (producer, date, access, distinguishing detail) directly, without a named template

_feedback.correct: Right. Checking guidance, even general guidance rather than a direct example, takes less time under pressure than it looks like, and avoids the errors a guess introduces.

_incorrect.notFinal: Ask whether the action is based on a rule the style guide actually states, or on a guess at what looks close enough.

title: Referencing an unfamiliar source quickly
instruction: Put these steps for referencing an unfamiliar source under time pressure in order.

_items.text: Identify the four elements the source actually carries
Check general guidance for anything the elements do not cover
Write the citation using what you have found
Record the decision, in a note or source log, before moving on

_feedback.correct: Right. Elements first, then guidance for any gap, then the citation, then a record of the decision, in that order, even under time pressure.

_incorrect.notFinal: Identify what the source carries before checking guidance for what it does not; otherwise you are checking guidance for a gap you have not confirmed exists.

title: Citing a source close to a deadline
body:
{{learner-a}} finds an unfamiliar source the night before a deadline. {{learner-a}} picks the closest-looking template, fills in what fits, guesses the rest, and submits without writing down what was decided.

{{learner-b}} finds the same kind of source with the same deadline. {{learner-b}} spends two minutes identifying the four elements the source carries, then checks the style guide's general rule for the one element it is missing. {{learner-b}} writes the citation and adds a one-line note to a source log recording the decision, in case the same source type appears again.

title: Four things worth recording about a decision
instruction: Select each card to reveal something worth recording about a referencing decision.

_items.title: What the source was
_items.body: Enough detail to recognise the same source, or source type, if it appears again.

_items.title: What guidance you used
_items.body: The general rule or principle you applied, not just the result.

_items.title: What you guessed
_items.body: Anywhere you could not find guidance and made a judgement call, flagged so it can be checked later.

_items.title: The date of the decision
_items.body: Guidance can be updated; knowing when you decided helps you judge whether to check again.

title: Four ways time pressure causes errors
instruction: Select each heading to reveal a way time pressure causes referencing errors.

_items.title: Skipping an element
_items.body: Rushing can mean one of the four elements (producer, date, access, distinguishing detail) is never checked at all.

_items.title: Guessing instead of checking
_items.body: A guess at the closest template takes a similar amount of time to checking general guidance, but is far more likely to be wrong.

_items.title: No record kept
_items.body: A decision made under pressure and never written down has to be remade, and possibly re-guessed, next time.

_items.title: Copying a wrong precedent
_items.body: Reusing a citation seen elsewhere without checking it was correct repeats someone else's error.

title: Referencing under pressure
body:
Use this checklist when referencing an unfamiliar source under time pressure:

  1. Identify the four elements the source actually carries.
  2. Check general guidance for anything the elements do not cover.
  3. Write the citation using what you have found.
  4. Record the decision before moving on.

title: Check your understanding
body: You have ten minutes before a submission deadline and an unfamiliar source to cite. What is the most efficient correct approach?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: Identify the source's four elements quickly, check general guidance for any gap, and cite it
Pick the closest-looking template and fill in the gaps without checking
Omit the citation and add it after submission
Cite it exactly as a similar source was cited elsewhere, without checking that citation's accuracy

_feedback.correct: Right. The four-element approach is quick enough for ten minutes and avoids the errors a guessed template or an uncritical copy would introduce.
_feedback._incorrect: Guessing, omitting, or copying an unchecked precedent are all faster only in appearance; each risks an error the four-element check would have caught.

title: Check your understanding
body: You are unsure how to cite a source and cannot find a direct example in the style guide. The guide does state a general rule covering this case. What should you do?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: Apply the general rule the guide states, even without a direct worked example
Guess, since no direct example exists for this source
Wait until a direct example becomes available before citing the source
Use a citation for an unrelated source type, since none matches exactly

_feedback.correct: Right. A general rule that covers the case is guidance, not a gap; applying it is checking guidance, not guessing.
_feedback._incorrect: A general rule that covers the case means guidance exists, even without a direct worked example; guessing, waiting, or substituting an unrelated citation all bypass guidance that was there to check.

title: Check your understanding
body: You make a referencing decision for {{context}} under time pressure, with no direct precedent to follow. What should you do afterwards?
instruction: Choose the best answer.

_items.text: Record the decision, including what guidance or judgement you used, so it can be repeated or corrected
Move on; the citation is written, so nothing further is needed
Delete any note of the decision, since it was made under pressure and may be wrong
Wait for someone else to check it before recording anything

_feedback.correct: Right. A decision made under pressure, with no direct precedent, is exactly the kind worth recording: it lets you or someone else repeat it correctly, or correct it, without starting from nothing.
_feedback._incorrect: Moving on, deleting the note, or waiting for someone else all lose the record a later check, or a later repeat of the same source, would need.

title: Supporting or challenging?
body: For each source description, decide whether it supports or challenges the position: structured revision timetables improve exam performance.
instruction: Match each source to the correct category.

_items.text: A study finding students who used structured timetables scored higher on average.
A study finding no significant difference between timetabled and self-paced revision.
A study finding rigid timetables increased reported stress without improving scores.
A survey where high-performing students reported using detailed revision schedules.

_feedback.correct: That is the pattern a reader needs to see: your reference list should carry sources like the challenging ones here, not just the supporting ones.

_incorrect.notFinal: Check what the finding actually shows, not just its topic. A study can discuss revision timetables and still challenge the position that they improve performance.

title: Building a balanced reference list
body: Put these steps in the order you would follow to build a balanced reference list for an argument.
instruction: Drag the steps into the correct order.

_items.text: State the position you intend to argue.
Search for sources that support that position.
Search separately for sources that challenge it, using terms that would surface disagreement.
Check that both lists are genuinely about the same question, not a related one.
Cite sources from both lists, with enough detail that a reader can trace each one.

_feedback.correct: Searching for challenging sources separately, using different search terms, is what stops a reference list defaulting to one-sided.

_incorrect.notFinal: The supporting search and the challenging search need to happen as two separate steps. Searching only once, for the position itself, tends to surface only sources that agree with it.

title: Worked example: arguing that group work improves learning outcomes

_items.title: Weaker approach
_items.body: {{learner-a}} wants to argue that group work improves learning outcomes. {{learner-a}} searches for "benefits of group work" and cites the first four relevant results, all of which find a positive effect. The reference list reads as one-sided, even though every citation is accurate, because no search was made for research finding no effect or a negative one.

_items.title: Stronger approach
_items.body: {{learner-b}} makes the same argument but runs two searches: one for studies finding group work improves outcomes, and a separate one for studies finding it has no effect or a negative one, using terms such as "group work drawbacks" and "free-rider effect". {{learner-b}} cites three supporting sources and two challenging ones, addressing the challenging findings directly in the argument rather than ignoring them.

title: Four signs a reference list is one-sided
displayTitle: Four signs a reference list is one-sided
body: Flip each card to see a sign that a reference list may be missing opposing evidence.
instruction: Select a card to reveal more detail.

_items.title: Every source agrees
_items.back: If every cited source reaches the same conclusion, the search likely stopped as soon as supporting evidence was found.

_items.title: One search term used
_items.back: Searching only for terms that match the position, rather than its opposite, tends to surface only agreeing sources.

_items.title: No counter-evidence addressed
_items.back: If the writing never mentions a finding that goes against the argument, a reader cannot tell whether one was looked for.

_items.title: All sources from one field
_items.back: Opposing evidence sometimes comes from a different discipline asking the same question; checking only one field's literature can miss it.

title: Why citing both sides matters
body: Expand each heading to see why research breadth matters to different readers.
instruction: Select a heading to expand it.

_items.title: For a marker
_items.body: A marker reading a one-sided reference list may read it as a sign the writer did not look for, or did not understand, the counter-evidence.

_items.title: For a peer reviewer
_items.body: A peer reviewer expects a literature review to represent the state of a field, not one side of a debate within it.

_items.title: For your own argument
_items.body: Addressing a counter-argument directly, with a citation behind it, is usually more persuasive than a reader discovering it was never considered.

_items.title: For future use of your work
_items.body: A balanced reference list remains useful to you later, when the same debate resurfaces in a different piece of work.

title: Checklist: gathering sources for both sides
displayTitle: Checklist: gathering sources for both sides
body:
• State the position in one sentence before searching.
  • Run a separate search for sources that challenge the position, using different search terms.
  • Check the challenging sources address the same question, not a related one.
  • Cite at least one source from each side with enough detail to trace it.
  • Address the challenging evidence directly in the text, rather than only in the reference list.

title: Check 1
instruction: A reference list cites six sources, all of which support the writer's position. What does this most likely indicate?

_items.text: The search was thorough and found strong agreement in the field.
The search likely stopped once supporting evidence was found, missing opposing evidence.
The topic has no genuine debate, so no opposing sources exist.
The writer should add more supporting sources to strengthen the list.

_feedback.correct: Six sources agreeing is far more often a sign the search stopped early than a sign of genuine consensus. A reader cannot tell the difference without seeing an opposing search attempted.

_incorrect.notFinal: Consider what a reader assumes when every citation agrees: that either the field genuinely agrees, which is rare for an arguable position, or the search did not look for disagreement.

title: Check 2
instruction: A writer finds three sources supporting their position and no sources challenging it after one search. What should they do next?

_items.text: Conclude the position is uncontested and cite the three sources.
Run a further search using terms likely to surface disagreement before concluding there is none.
Add a fourth supporting source to strengthen the argument.
Remove the position from the argument since no challenge was found.

_feedback.correct: One search finding no opposing evidence usually means the search terms matched only the supporting side, not that no challenge exists. A further, differently worded search is needed before concluding the position is uncontested.

_incorrect.notFinal: One search returning only supporting sources is rarely proof that no opposing research exists. Think about what the search terms themselves might have missed.

title: Check 3
instruction: You are building a reference list for an argument in {{context}}. What is the clearest sign your reference list demonstrates research breadth rather than selective citation?

_items.text: It contains more sources overall than a classmate's reference list.
It cites at least one source that directly challenges the position, addressed in the text.
It cites only sources published in the last two years.
It cites sources from several different authors rather than one author repeatedly.

_feedback.correct: Research breadth is shown by engaging with opposing evidence, not by source count, recency or author variety alone. A reader looks for whether a challenging source is cited and addressed.

_incorrect.notFinal: Think about what a reader is actually checking for: not how many sources there are, but whether the writer engaged with evidence against their own position.
